summary: Surveys proposals made during an effort to address scalability, multihoming and inter-domain traffic engineering problems in Internet routing and addressing. It recommends directions the IETF might take. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet's routing system is running out of room. This memo reviews the many designs that were put forward to fix that, one by one, and ends with the recommendation of the two people who chaired the study: improve aggregation in the short term, adopt a clean split between an address and the place it lives, and make it cheap to change addresses.

subtitle: A survey of the proposals put forward to solve Internet routing scalability, and what the research group recommends.

tldr.problem: The Internet's routing and addressing architecture is under strain from three pressures: growth in the global routing table, sites that connect through more than one provider, and traffic engineering between domains.
tldr.mechanism: The document surveys the proposals brought to the Routing Research Group, giving each one a key idea, a list of gains, a list of costs, a critique from other members and a rebuttal from its authors.
tldr.outcome: The group never reached consensus, so the two co-chairs wrote the recommendation themselves: work on Evolution, on ILNP, and on making renumbering cheap and automatic.

today: RFC 6115 is an Informational document from February 2011, published by the Internet Research Task Force, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes it and none that updates it. It records the opinion of the research group's two co-chairs rather than a consensus of the group, and it asks the IETF to work on Evolution, on ILNP and on renumbering.

sections.title: The Problem and How the Research Group Worked
sections.content:
It is commonly recognized that the Internet routing and addressing architecture is facing challenges in scalability, multihoming and inter-domain traffic engineering. This document presents, as a recommendation of future directions for the IETF, solutions that could aid the future scalability of the Internet. To that end it surveys many of the proposals that were brought forward for discussion in this activity, as well as some of the subsequent analysis and the architectural recommendation of the chairs. It is a product of the Routing Research Group. Readers are cautioned not to draw any conclusions about the degree of interest or endorsement by the group from the presence of any proposal in the document, or from the amount of analysis devoted to it.

The group was chartered to research and recommend a new routing architecture for the Internet. The goal was to explore many alternatives and build consensus around a single proposal. The only constraint on its process was that the process be open and that the group set forth with the usual discussion of proposals and trying to build consensus around them. There were no explicit contingencies for the eventuality that the group did not reach consensus. The group met at every IETF meeting from March 2007 to March 2010 and discussed many proposals, in person and through its mailing list.

The group did not reach consensus. Rather than lose the contributions and progress that had been made, the chairs elected to collect the proposals of the group and some of the debate concerning them, and to make a recommendation from those proposals. The recommendation therefore reflects the opinions of the chairs and not necessarily the consensus of the group. The proposals were collected in an open call, after which the group was asked to self-organize to produce a single critique for each proposal, and the proponents were given the opportunity to write a rebuttal. No counterpoints to the rebuttals were submitted. All of the proposals were given the opportunity to progress their documents to RFC status, but not all have chosen to pursue that path, so some of the references in the document may become inaccessible. The group did reach consensus that the overall document should be published.
sections.plainLanguage: The study was meant to pick one design and agree on it. It did not manage that. Instead, the two chairs took the best material, wrote a review of each proposal with its strengths, its costs and the objections raised against it, and then made a recommendation of their own. So the last word in the document belongs to them, not to the group.

sections.title: What Everyone Agreed to Call Things
sections.content:
The group reached broad and clear consensus on some terminology and several important technical points, and the document records them for posterity.

A node is either a host or a router. A router is any device that forwards packets at the network layer of the Internet architecture, such as IPv4 or IPv6. A host is a device that can send or receive packets to and from the network but does not forward packets. A bridge is a device that forwards packets at the link layer, such as Ethernet; an Ethernet switch or hub is an example.

An address is an object that combines aspects of identity with topological location, and IPv4 and IPv6 addresses are current examples. A locator is a structured, topology-dependent name that is not used for node identification and is not a path; it is either the topology-dependent name of a node's interface, or the topology-dependent name of a single subnetwork or of a group of related subnetworks that share a single aggregate, of which an IP routing prefix is a current example. An identifier is a topology-independent name for a logical node, which might be a single physical device, a cluster of devices acting as a single node, or a single virtual partition of a single physical device. An OSI End System Identifier is an example of an identifier, and so is a Fully Qualified Domain Name that precisely names one logical node, though not all FQDNs meet that definition. Various other names, other than addresses, locators or identifiers, may exist at various protocol layers, each with the sole purpose of identifying a component of a logical system or physical device.

On the technical points, the group had rough consensus that separating identity from location is desirable and technically feasible, but it did not have consensus on the best engineering approach to such a split. It had consensus that the Internet needs to support multihoming in a manner that scales well and does not have prohibitive costs, and that any IETF solution to Internet scaling has to not only support multihoming but address the real-world constraints of end customers, large and small.
sections.plainLanguage: Before comparing designs, the group agreed on three words. An address mixes who you are with where you are. A locator says where something is, and changes when it moves. An identifier says who something is, and does not change when it moves. Most of the proposals are about using identifiers and locators separately instead of fusing them into one address.

sections.title: The Map-and-Encap Proposals
sections.content:
The first family of proposals, described in sections 2 to 13 of the document, keeps today's Internet in place and adds a mapping system and tunnels around it. LISP (section 2) is the best known. It implements a locator/identifier separation mechanism using encapsulation between routers at the edge of the Internet. Such a separation allows topological aggregation of the routable addresses, the locators, while providing stable and portable numbering of end systems, the identifiers.

LISP's listed gains are extensive: topological aggregation of the locator space used for routing, which greatly reduces both the overall size and the churn rate of the information needed to operate the global routing system; a separate identifier space for end systems, effectively allowing provider-independent addressing for all without adding state to the global routing system; improved traffic engineering that explicitly does not add state to the global routing system; no changes required to end systems; no changes to core routers; minimal and straightforward changes to edge routers; and a defined router-to-router protocol, mapping system, deployment plan and interworking mechanisms.

The listed costs are infrastructure: a mapping system of map servers, map resolvers and Alternative Logical Topology routers, and interworking infrastructure in the form of proxy ingress tunnel routers, both described as new potential business opportunities. The third cost is the overhead of determining and maintaining whether a locator or path is still alive, which the document notes is a common issue for all identifier and locator separation proposals.

The group's critique of LISP is that a global query server network means long paths and a real risk of packet loss, so an ingress tunnel router with no mapping drops the first packets of a session and waits for the client to resend. ALT's aggressively aggregated structure makes those paths intercontinental. On multihoming, the ITRs have to test reachability of end-user networks through two or more egress tunnel routers, which is inefficient, and the ITRs cannot test network reachability themselves because they do not hold an address inside each ETR's network, so the ETRs have to report unreachability. LISP involves complex communication between ITRs and ETRs, with UDP and 64-bit LISP headers on all traffic packets. In LISP's mobility approach each mobile node needs a routing locator address to be its own ETR, so the node cannot be behind a NAT, and mapping changes must reach all relevant ITRs instantly every time the node gets a new address, which LISP cannot achieve. The authors replied that initial packet loss and delay turn out not to be a deep issue, since mechanisms for interoperation with the legacy network are needed in any viably deployable design and LISP has them, and that ALT is not mandatory as the long-term mapping system because LISP has a standardized mapping system interface.

The other proposals in this family differ in the details. Ivip (section 4) is a core-edge separation scheme for IPv4 and IPv6 with a mapping distribution network structured like a cross-linked multicast tree, pushing every mapping change to full-database query servers within a few seconds. CRM (section 7) builds a highly scalable mapping system using compact routing principles, with map servers assigned as cluster heads or landmarks based on their ability to aggregate endpoint identifier announcements. LMS (section 8) builds a hierarchical mapping system with a two-cache mechanism on the ingress tunnel router, with tunnelling and mapping done at the core and no change on edge networks. TIDR (section 11) enriches BGP with new attributes so that identifier prefixes are not installed in the routing table but moved to a Tunnel Information Base, so that the packet is tunnelled to the tail end of the tunnel and routed by the routers in between. EEMDP (section 13) looks at how mapping distribution protocols handle subprefixes spread across several egress tunnel routers and multihoming with a hierarchy of egress routers.
sections.plainLanguage: The first family keeps the Internet as it is and bolts a mapping system onto the edge. Traffic to an address the network has never seen is wrapped in a tunnel to the real destination, and a lookup tells the edge router where that is. LISP is the leading example: the gain is that the addresses in the global routing table can be aggregated, and the cost is new infrastructure to run the lookups.

sections.title: Proposals That Change the Architecture
sections.content:
The second family does not tunnel around the existing Internet; it changes how the stack is built. ILNP, the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol, described in section 12, gives a crisp separation of identifiers from locators. Identifiers name nodes, not interfaces, and locators name subnetworks rather than interfaces, so they are equivalent to an IP routing prefix. Identifiers are never used for network-layer routing, and locators are never used for node identity. Transport-layer sessions, such as TCP session state, use only identifiers, so a change of location has no adverse impact on an IP session. Its listed benefits include fully scalable site and node multihoming, site and node mobility, topological aggregation of location information that reduces both the prefix churn rate and the size of the global routing table, improved traffic engineering without adding state to the global routing system, elimination of triangle routing in all cases, and incremental deployability with no changes required to existing IPv6 or IPv4 routers.

RANGI (section 3), similar to the Host Identity Protocol, introduces a host identifier layer between the network layer and the transport layer, so that transport-layer associations are bound to host identifiers rather than IP addresses. Its identifier is a 128-bit hierarchical and cryptographic identifier with organizational structure, and its locators are IPv4-embedded IPv6 addresses. hIPv4 (section 5) splits IPv4 address space into a globally unique area locator and a regionally unique endpoint locator, carried in a shim header between the IP header and the transport header, with a new element in the service provider's routing domain called a Locator Swap Router, and no new routing protocols or mapping systems. NOL (section 6) adds a name overlay on top of the existing TCP/IP stack, managing host name configuration, registration and authentication, initiating and managing connections by name, and keeping application data transport continuity for mobility.

GLI-Split (section 10) separates global routing from local routing using global and local locators, plus a separate static identifier, with locators and identifiers encoded in IPv6 addresses so that the IPv6 Internet keeps working. Two-Phased Mapping (section 9) splits the mapping in two: a prefix to autonomous system number mapping, and an autonomous system number to egress tunnel routers mapping, with all mapping information collected locally and phase one information held in a registry organized like DNS. Name-Based Sockets (section 15) move the indirection from domain names to IP addresses out of applications and down into the IP layer, so that applications communicate by domain name only. IRON-RANGER (section 16) builds on the RANGER design for global enterprise recursion. Evolution (section 14) takes a different tack: rather than a new architecture, it improves aggregation where it is cheapest, with aggregation at increasing scopes, and the argument that any solution will start with one or a few early adopters and may never reach the whole Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The second family changes the building blocks instead of working around them. ILNP, which the chairs later recommend, gives every node a permanent identifier and every network a locator, and lets the transport layer use the identifier so that moving a node does not break its sessions. Others change the address format, add a name layer, or simply improve how well addresses can be grouped together.

sections.title: The Recommendation to the IETF
sections.content:
As can be seen from the extensive list of proposals, the group explored a number of possible solutions, but it did not reach rough consensus on a single best approach. The recommendation was therefore left to the co-chairs. The goal of the research group was to develop a recommendation for an approach to a routing and addressing architecture for the Internet, and the primary goal of that architecture is to provide improved scalability for the routing subsystem: to continue growing the routing subsystem to meet the needs of the Internet without drastic and continuous increases in the amount of state or processing required by routers.

The motivation is a general concern that the cost and structure of the routing and addressing architecture as it is today may become prohibitively expensive with continued growth, with repercussions for the health of the Internet, so there is an urgent need to examine and evaluate potential scalability enhancements. For the long term, IPv6 is going to play a significant role; it has taken more than a decade, but IPv6 is starting to see some non-trivial amount of deployment, in part because of the depletion of IPv4 addresses. The new architecture must therefore be applicable to IPv6, since the two share a common routing architecture.

Whatever change is made should be expected to be a very long-lived change, and permanent, pervasive changes to a loosely coordinated, complex and expensive subsystem require difficult choices during deployment and integration. If the community is going to the trouble, pain and expense of major architectural changes, it should aim for long-term solutions that place the network in the best possible position for ongoing growth, with the new elements integrated cleanly as first-class citizens on a par with the existing legacy primitives. The Internet's history is full of temporary, ad-hoc changes with significant long-term maintenance and architectural complexity, which is to be avoided. The chairs therefore believe the situation requires pursuing both short-term improvements and long-term solutions: the short-term improvements are to be completely localized and temporary, giving time to develop, test and deploy the long-term solution, and they can be withdrawn as the long-term solution gains traction.

The recommendation to the IETF is to pursue work in three areas: Evolution, the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol, and renumbering. Evolution was selected because it is a short-term improvement that can be applied on a per-domain basis, under local administration, with immediate effect, and can be deployed by domains that feel it necessary for as long as they feel it necessary. ILNP was recommended because it is a clean solution for the architecture: it separates location from identity in a clear, straightforward way that is consistent with the remainder of the Internet architecture and makes both first-class citizens, and unlike the many map-and-encap proposals there are no complications due to tunnelling, indirection, or semantics that shift over the lifetime of a packet's delivery. Further work on automating renumbering is recommended because even with ILNP, the ability of a domain to change its locators at minimal cost is fundamentally necessary: no routing architecture will scale without some form of abstraction, and domains that change their point of attachment must be prepared to change their locators in line with that abstraction.
sections.plainLanguage: The chairs make three asks. Improve aggregation now, because it can be done by one domain at a time and buys time. Build ILNP, because it puts identifiers and locators in the architecture itself rather than bolting a tunnel on top. And make renumbering cheap and automatic, because a domain that moves will have to change its locators no matter which architecture is chosen.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Space precludes a full treatment of security considerations for all proposals summarized in the document, following the guidance of RFC 3552. However, it was a requirement of the research group to provide security that is at least as strong as the existing Internet routing and addressing architecture. Each technical proposal has slightly different security considerations, the details of which are in the references cited.
sections.plainLanguage: The document does not work through the security questions for each proposal, because there was no room. It states the rule instead: whatever is built has to be no weaker than what the Internet has today.

viz.caption: A SELECTION OF THE PROPOSALS, EACH IN ONE LINE

items.title: LISP
items.text: Encapsulates traffic between edge routers, so locators aggregate while end systems keep stable identifiers.

items.title: Ivip
items.text: A core-edge separation scheme for IPv4 and IPv6 with a fast-push mapping distribution network.

items.title: CRM
items.text: A highly scalable mapping system built on compact routing, with map servers as cluster heads.

items.title: LMS
items.text: A hierarchical mapping system with a two-cache mechanism on the ingress tunnel router.

items.title: TIDR
items.text: Tunnels between edge routers, with new BGP attributes carrying the identifier-to-locator mappings.

items.title: RANGI
items.text: A host identifier layer between network and transport, with a 128-bit hierarchical identifier.

items.title: hIPv4
items.text: IPv4 address space split into a global area locator and a regional endpoint locator.

items.title: ILNP
items.text: Identifiers name nodes and locators name subnetworks, with no tunnelling at all.
